body:
Thank you for your effort, but I doubt this approach can be considered correct. It's not so much that you're hardcoding the method list on the GDScript side, but that most of the methods you listed **can return `null`**.

<details>
<summary>List</summary>

---

### Array

> * `.back()`
> * `.front()`

> If the array is empty, fails and returns null

---

> * `.get()`

> If index out-of-bounds or negative, this method fails and returns null

---

> * `.max()`
> * `.min()`

> Otherwise, returns null

---

> * .pick_random()

> Generates an error and returns null if the array is empty

---

> * `.pop_at()`
> * `.pop_back()`
> * `.pop_front()`

> Returns null if the array is empty

---

### Dictionary

> * .find_key()

> Finds and returns ..., or null if it is not found

---

> * .get()

> Returns ..., or null if the parameter is omitted

---

> * `.get_or_add()`

This is potentially possible, but the problem is that you have to change not only the type of the `default` parameter, but also its default value.

```
Variant get_or_add(key: Variant, default: Variant = null)
                                                  ^^^^^^
```

---

</details>

The problem is that **only `Object` and its descendants are nullable**. All other types don't accept `null`. Therefore, the following example violates the static typing and the guarantees on which GDScript VM relies for validated call optimizations:

```gdscript
var dict: Dictionary[String, String]
# Returns `null` at runtime, but the line is marked as safe
# and GDScript VM assumes that this is impossible.
var key: String = dict.find_key("non-existent")
```

Also, nullable and union types currently do not exist in the core and GDScript; you can't mark the return type as `int?` or `int|Nil` instead of `int`. The closest existing type to `int|Nil` is `Variant`. 

So I think we'd better wait for a properly implemented unified type system with support for nullable and union types in the core before trying to implement this on the GDScript side.

This could potentially be solved using runtime wrappers or core-side array/dictionary type checks: returning the default value for that type instead of `null` (`false` for `bool`, `0` for `int`, `Callable()` for `Callable`, and so on). However, this has a runtime cost and breaks compatibility (it changes the value the method returns on failure).

> The problem is that only Object and its descendants are nullable. All other types don't accept null.

Ah of course, that makes sense now that you said it. I believe this hasn't been mentioned in the related issues before so I didn't think of it.

> So I think we'd better wait for a properly implemented unified type system with support for nullable and union types in the core before trying to implement this on the GDScript side.

Agreed for most of the methods. However, what if I modified the PR to just fix the return types for `dict.values()` and `dict.keys()` methods? The problem you mentioned doesn't exist for those. :thinking:

I agree that implementing the return values for `dict.values()` and `dict.keys()` now, since we already can, would be a good idea. 
The rest of the return typing will have to wait for nullable types. Related PR #76843
I cleaned up the PR to only fix the return types of `dict.keys()` and `dict.values()`. What do you think?

> However, what if I modified the PR to just fix the return types for `dict.values()` and `dict.keys()` methods? The problem you mentioned doesn't exist for those.

Yes, this is possible and doesn't seem to have any obvious dangerous consequences. But here we're entering the shaky ground of sophistic arguments and personal opinions. Should we add exceptions (even useful ones) if we can't implement them for all "generic" methods of typed arrays and dictionaries? What's more important to us, convenience or consistency? Users might ask us why we implemented this only for `keys()` and `values()` and not for other methods.

As for more practical arguments, I'll list the following:

1. The documentation and `PropertyInfo` reflection don't have parameter types for "generic" methods. The return type is displayed as `Array`, not `Array[TKey]` and `Array[TValue]`. Therefore, we need to specifically state in the description, "In GDScript, the return type is actually...".
2. This only affects GDScript, not the core, GDExtension, or C#. This is a disturbing precedent. GDScript relies heavily on the core and very rarely attempts to override its behavior, especially when it comes to the type system. Yes, we have some tweaks for the editor, but I don't recall such a precedent for the analyzer.

Looking at [dictionary.cpp](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/core/variant/dictionary.cpp), I can see that [keys()](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/core/variant/dictionary.cpp#L380) and [values()](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/master/core/variant/dictionary.cpp#L400) already return typed arrays if the dictionary is typed, so looks to me like GDScript is missing this functionality, and this PR wouldn't be adding anything "new". 
I don't know how C# and GDExtension handle this typed return.

> This only affects GDScript, not the core, GDExtension, or C#. This is a disturbing precedent. GDScript relies heavily on the core and very rarely attempts to override its behavior, especially when it comes to the type system. Yes, we have some tweaks for the editor, but I don't recall such a precedent for the analyzer.

This is a good point and I understand the case for slippery slope here in terms of codebase quality.

What I haven't yet understood is why do `TypedArray[]` and `TypedDictionary[]` operators have proper typing in GDScript and the methods not, what is the case for them to have this exception (if it is an exception)?

> and this PR wouldn't be adding anything "new"

The "new" thing is that GDScript, in a few exceptional cases, doesn't rely on the type information returned by the core, but instead "invents" the missing details itself.

If your boss gives you imprecise instructions and you have no way to communicate this, you have two options: follow them verbatim or invent what they meant. Which would you choose if the first option is clearly acceptable (even if imperfect), while the second places responsibility on you for your initiative? The analogy is imprecise, but in many cases, compilers and other software tools often prefer to be literal and not invent things that aren't their responsibility.

> What I haven't yet understood is why do `TypedArray[]` and `TypedDictionary[]` operators have proper typing in GDScript and the methods not, what is the case for them to have this exception (if it is an exception)?

The assignment and subscript operators, as well as the array/dictionary construction syntax (`[]` and `{}`) have been this way since 4.0; it's established behavior and is more a language-specific feature (you can't overload operators in GDScript and you can't get the operator's `MethodInfo` to check). Meanwhile, methods are more a core API feature than a language-specific feature. This is the new behavior you're proposing for 4.6. If you look at the [`TypedArray`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/4ad11b6af38cd16a21d1bf3e737cebc5f0e91f6b/core/variant/typed_array.h#L40-L63) and [`TypedDictionary`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/4ad11b6af38cd16a21d1bf3e737cebc5f0e91f6b/core/variant/typed_dictionary.h#L40-L69) classes in C++, you'll only see constructors and operators, not methods.
Thanks for the thorough explanations. It seems that there are no low hanging fruits here. It's ok to close the PR if you think the same. :pray:

Ok so I've been looking into how we could handle it core-side and it doesn't seem currently possible (to me), due to the way method info is implemented. The method info is static but this would be dynamic, which obviously don't work together. Compile time vs runtime and all that.

An analyzer filling in the runtime information would be the only way to accomplish this (as far as I can tell), and I do agree that it isn't "literal", as you describe Danil, which is not ideal. 
However, I would argue it is completely safe and thus should be implemented because of the merits, namely help for people who do strong typing, which outweigh the issue of not being literal. 
That would indeed introduce a new "behavior" to the analyzer though, which would need some discussion. @vnen what would be your quick opinion on the matter?
